synopsis: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027 and places self-evolving ML safety components on a notified-body route, but whether trained-then-frozen perception qualifies is disputed; notified-body positions were not found, and Chapter 12 acknowledges reliance on secondary rather than verified primary wording [f12407, f2091, f11187, f10308]. The corpus repeatedly gives 2 August 2028 for machinery-related high-risk AI obligations, while also reporting removal from direct AI Act high-risk classification and a shift to Machinery Regulation delegated acts, which had not been adopted by 1 October 2026 [f53, f10453, f2095, f2096, f2098]. Notified-body lead time could exceed the four-month validation window, but published lead-time evidence was not found; an early opinion on frozen-model classification is recommended, with absent pre-consultation by early 2027 identified as a warning sign [f364, f259, f7436, f10786]. Deterministic radar or cooperative channels can limit what ML perception must prove, but the glossary makes differing failure modes a condition; a non-ML safety-channel option is recommended to reduce regulatory rejection risk [f676, f12122, f11058]. ML perception needs separate assurance because physics-based FDA/V&V 40 methods exclude it, and formal or static verification alone cannot establish recognition of arbitrary real scenes [f8220, f1025]. The standards landscape remains incomplete: ML safety standards are mostly draft, ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 is guidance rather than a requirement, and ISO/PAS 8800:2024 is road-vehicle-only; UL 4600 instead requires a safety case to address or explicitly argue away ML and other assurance prompts [f2099, f2100, f2101, f2102, f12263].
